author: Sandy Harjo Livingston
title: TFA sees 43% increase, Hawaiʻi locals moving back home - NewsBreak
text:
By Sandy Harjo Livingston ,
11 hours ago
HONOLULU (KHON2) — Young people want work that matters. They are asking hard questions about purpose, stability and impact; and for many, the answer is a classroom.
Teach For America (TFA) reported a 43% increase in its teaching corps this year, Take this alongside its growth in their Ignite tutoring fellowship, and we see a sign that more young professionals are choosing careers grounded in purpose and community impact.
In Hawaiʻi, that growth feels personal.
Meilan Akaka Manfre, Executive Director for Teach For America Hawaiʻi, knows the path well because she walked it.
“Teach for America is a national nonprofit committed to ensuring all kids have access to an excellent education,” she explained. “My leadership journey began as a core member in 2008. Teach for America paved the way for me to come back home from the continent to serve at James Campbell High School, our largest public high school in the state, to serve and teach 9th and 10th grade math as a special education teacher.”
The organization launched in Hawaiʻi in 2006 to bring college graduates to teach for at least two years in public schools.
Manfre said she ended up staying five years and later served as special education department head.
Since 2006, there have been 257 Native Hawaiian corps members who have joined TFA Hawaiʻi. Manfre said she wants people to see teaching as both a way to come home and a way to stay.
“I really want folks to know that TFA is a path to come back home, to teach or stay home to teach and have this teaching experience be a catalyst for a career,” she said.
Across the country, more than 5,500 college students have served as Ignite tutors since 2020. More than 550 of those tutors have gone on to join the teaching corps.
Manfre pointed to the Ignite fellowship as more than a tutoring program. She described it as a deliberate bridge that allows aspiring educators to test their commitment in real classrooms while building the skills and confidence to lead their own.
“It’s a really great gateway to provide an opportunity to work directly with our keiki here and then build that from that success to launch their career in education as core members,” she said.
Tutoring that meets families where they are
Ignite provides high dosage tutoring during the school day at four public schools, including Nānākuli and Waiʻanae. Students do not pay for this academic service, andf families don’t need to adjust after school schedules since. Tutors align their lessons with classroom curriculum.
“We recruit and train folks to provide real, live tutoring within the school day in our partner public schools,” Manfre said.
Manfre said early results point to measurable academic growth on I Ready assessments, along with another shift that matters just as much to educators and families: students are showing up more consistently and feeling more connected to their campuses.
“We’re also seeing student satisfaction rates where they’re deepening their sense of belonging at school, and their attendance to school is actually higher on their Ignite tutoring days,” she explained.
For those standing at a career crossroads and weighing whether the classroom is the right place to begin, Manfre framed TFA as both a proving ground and a community, one designed to surround new educators with shared purpose and daily, tangible impact.
“Teach for America provides that path to be in a cohort of likeminded individuals with diverse backgrounds, committed to connecting with one another, connecting to our community and having meaningful impact with our keiki every single day,” she said.
The deadline to apply to the FTA corps is March 9. The Ignite fellowship deadline is April 29.

“Whether it’s through the classroom or through volunteerism or through philanthropic gifts, you can play a role,” Manfre said. “And I invite you to play a role with us.”
